title: Evaling Video Slop — Maor Bril, Character.ai

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: Media & Creative
domains.rationale: The entire talk concerns evaluating AI-generated video—a core creative media application. Character.ai produces character-based video content, and the evaluation addresses storytelling, visual coherence, and audio-visual sync.

summary: Maor Bril, Principal Software Engineer at Character.ai, presents "Evaling Video Slop" at AI Engineer World's Fair 2026. The talk addresses the critical gap between AI video generation quality and evaluation methodology. While models like Kling, Sora, VEO, and SeaDance produce visually impressive video at near-zero cost, most outputs still contain hallucinations—extra limbs, impossible physics, hovering characters, unsynced audio—that existing evaluation tools fail to catch. CLIP score evaluates single frames but misses temporal incoherence; LPIPS detects inter-frame drift but cannot assess story quality. Bril argues video is fundamentally a storytelling medium requiring evaluation across story fidelity, physics, pacing, character consistency, and audio-visual synchronization. The team's first iteration combined frame-level metrics, a consistent LLM-as-judge, and human annotation into a repeatable benchmark, but it was too slow and expensive for near-user generation. The key insight was catching drift early—before short clips are stitched into longer videos. They distilled a committee of expert evaluators into one small, fast VLM (Qwen, chosen for strong post-training experience) that scores a 15-second video in approximately 3 seconds and explains why a video is bad rather than returning only a binary verdict. The most important conceptual shift was from absolute scoring (1–10) to pairwise comparison (is B a better story than A), because inter-rater agreement is much higher on relative judgments. Training data was built by manufacturing badness—corrupting good videos and generating random slop—and pairing real footage against AI footage with consistent encoding and identical annotation to prevent the model from becoming an AI detector. V1 was confidently wrong: it awarded 9.2 for camera work on a four-second frozen frame and praised physics on hovering ghosts, because it learned to reward gloss and vibe rather than substance. Bril's closing advice: score the real axes you care about explicitly, put eval inside the generation loop, and evaluate video as a story. In Q&A, he covers sound evaluation via Atmos and key-frame timestamp matching, lip syncing as unsolved, human calibration sessions (10–15 minutes annotating random axes), Qwen selection rationale, and unit economics of scaling the judge as a tradeoff between a small served model and a slower expert cohort. The open-source JudgeJudy harness connects arbitrary agents or LLMs as video quality judges with custom rubrics, automated metrics, and human calibration.
whyItMatters: These concepts form a coherent methodology for evaluating AI-generated video at production scale. The talk traces a clear arc: (1) the problem—frame-level metrics (CLIP, LPIPS) fail because video is a storytelling medium requiring temporal, physics, pacing, and audio evaluation; (2) the approach—distilling a committee of expert evaluators into a small fast VLM judge trained on pairwise preferences with Bradley-Terry loss; (3) the data engineering—manufacturing badness by corrupting good videos and pairing real vs. AI footage to prevent AI-detector degeneration; (4) the deployment—integrating eval inside the generation loop as a CI regression gate for early drift detection; (5) the scaling—unit economics tradeoffs between a small served model and a slower expert cohort. Each concept builds on the previous one: the failure of frame-level metrics motivates pairwise comparison, which requires careful training data construction, which must be deployed inside the generation loop for early detection, and which must scale economically. The V1 confident failure (rewarding gloss over substance) serves as the cautionary tale that ties these together: without scoring real axes explicitly and putting eval in the loop, even a well-designed judge can produce dangerously misleading high-confidence outputs.
temporalContext: The talk was published on YouTube on July 25, 2026, and was presented at AI Engineer World's Fair 2026. JudgeJudy was open-sourced on March 26, 2026. Research was conducted as of August 22, 2026. Character.ai CEO Karandeep Anand was appointed June 2025. The video generation models discussed (Kling, Sora, VEO, SeaDance) represent the state of AI video generation as of mid-2026.
takeaways: Video generation is cheap and good; evaluating video quality is the hard, unsolved part.
Frame-level metrics like CLIP score and LPIPS cannot assess story coherence, pacing, physics, or audio sync across time.
Pairwise comparison (is B better than A) is more reliable than absolute scoring because humans agree more on relative quality.
A small VLM judge (Qwen) can score a 15-second video in ~3 seconds, balancing speed and accuracy better than a larger model.
V1 failed confidently—scoring vibe and gloss over substance—because training data taught it to detect coherent-looking artifacts rather than genuine story quality.
Pairing real vs. AI footage with consistent encoding and identical annotation prevents the judge from becoming an AI detector.
Put eval inside the generation loop; catch drift early before clips are stitched into long-form video.
Sound evaluation combines Atmos for quality and key-frame timestamp matching to detect sound spikes at expected moments; lip syncing remains unsolved.
Human annotation sessions (10–15 min per person on random axes) calibrate AI judges and generate training data for the next model version.
Scaling the judge is a unit-economics tradeoff: a served small model wins at thousands of evaluations per day; a slower expert cohort suffices at smaller scale.

concepts.name: CLIP Score
concepts.explanation: CLIP score excels at evaluating individual frames by measuring alignment between visual and text embeddings, but it cannot assess temporal coherence, story quality, or audio-visual sync across a video.
concepts.importance: Illustrates the fundamental limitation of applying image-era metrics to video: frame-level quality does not imply video-level quality.

concepts.name: LPIPS
concepts.explanation: LPIPS (Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity) detects inter-frame drift by measuring perceptual distance between consecutive frames, but cannot judge whether a video tells a coherent story.
concepts.importance: Shows that even temporal-aware metrics miss the narrative dimension of video quality, motivating the need for story-level evaluation.

concepts.name: LLM-as-Judge
concepts.explanation: Using foundational LLMs as quality judges for video was attempted but found to be slow, prompt-dependent, and inconsistent across different users, motivating distillation into a smaller specialized model.
concepts.importance: Highlights the practical limitations of using general-purpose LLMs for evaluation at scale, driving the design of a faster, more consistent VLM judge.

concepts.name: Pairwise Preference Comparison
concepts.explanation: Instead of scoring videos on an absolute 1–10 scale (which produces low inter-rater agreement), the team asks whether video B tells a better story than video A, yielding much higher agreement and more robust training signal.
concepts.importance: The central methodological insight of the talk: relative comparison produces more reliable quality judgments than absolute scoring for subjective video quality.

concepts.name: Bradley-Terry Loss
concepts.explanation: The pairwise preference judge is trained using Bradley-Terry loss, a ranking loss that models the probability that one item is preferred over another, enabling preference-based fine-tuning of the VLM.
concepts.importance: Connects the pairwise comparison methodology to a concrete training objective, making the approach reproducible.

concepts.name: VLM Judge (Vision-Language Model)
concepts.explanation: A small vision-language model (Qwen-family) was distilled from a committee of expert evaluators to score a 15-second video in approximately 3 seconds and explain why a video is bad rather than returning only a binary verdict.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates how to deploy fast, interpretable video quality evaluation by distilling expertise into a single efficient model.

concepts.name: Manufacturing Badness
concepts.explanation: Training data for the VLM judge was constructed by corrupting good videos and generating random slop, creating negative examples paired against real footage with consistent encoding and identical annotation to prevent the model from degenerating into an AI detector.
concepts.importance: Reveals a practical data engineering strategy for building evaluation training sets without large-scale human labeling.

concepts.name: AI Detector Degeneration
concepts.explanation: When training pairs distinguish real footage from AI footage, the model can degenerate into an AI detector (classifying provenance rather than quality) instead of judging story quality; consistent encoding and identical annotation on both sides mitigate this.
concepts.importance: Identifies a critical failure mode in training video quality judges and the data design principle that prevents it.

concepts.name: Temporal Consistency
concepts.explanation: Video evaluation must account for coherence across time: character consistency across shots, physics plausibility throughout the clip, and pacing—none of which frame-level metrics can capture.
concepts.importance: Defines the multi-dimensional quality space that video evaluation must cover beyond single-frame aesthetics.

concepts.name: Audio-Visual Sync via Atmos and Key-Frame Timestamp Matching
concepts.explanation: Sound quality is evaluated using Atmos for intelligibility, and audio-visual synchronization is checked by matching sound spikes at key-frame timestamps—when the prompt says 'the door slammed,' the model looks for a sound spike at the corresponding timestamp.
concepts.importance: Provides a concrete methodology for evaluating the audio dimension of video quality, which existing metrics ignore entirely.

concepts.name: Absolute vs. Relative Scoring
concepts.explanation: Absolute 1–10 scoring collapses quality to a single dimension with low inter-rater agreement, while pairwise comparison (is B better than A) preserves nuance and yields high agreement because humans are better at relative than absolute judgment.
concepts.importance: The core insight driving the entire evaluation redesign: comparison is more robust than scoring for subjective quality.

concepts.name: Model Distillation (Committee to Single VLM)
concepts.explanation: A committee of expert evaluators (foundational models) was distilled into one small, fast VLM that retains enough accuracy for production use while scoring 15-second videos in approximately 3 seconds.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates a practical distillation strategy for deploying evaluation at production speed and scale.

concepts.name: Confident Failure in V1 Judge
concepts.explanation: V1 of the judge was confidently wrong: it scored 9.2 on camera work for a four-second frozen frame and praised physics on hovering ghosts, because training data taught it to reward surface gloss and vibe rather than whether the story was actually told.
concepts.importance: Illustrates how evaluation models can overfit to surface features and produce dangerously misleading high-confidence scores.

concepts.name: Video as Storytelling Medium
concepts.explanation: Bril argues that video is fundamentally a storytelling medium, so evaluation must cover story fidelity, physics, pacing, character consistency, and audio-visual synchronization—not just frame-level visual quality.
concepts.importance: Provides the conceptual foundation for why existing metrics fail and what a proper video evaluation must measure.

concepts.name: Qwen Model Selection
concepts.explanation: A Qwen-family vision-language model was selected as the judge backbone due to strong prior post-training experience, rather than exhaustive benchmarking; other models were tried but Qwen was good enough.
concepts.importance: Reveals that production model selection is often driven by practical experience and post-training capability rather than systematic comparison.

concepts.name: Lip Syncing Evaluation (Unsolved)
concepts.explanation: Lip syncing remains an unsolved problem in video evaluation, especially for animated talking characters whose mouth movement has no real correlation with speech audio.
concepts.importance: Identifies a frontier challenge in audio-visual evaluation that current VLM judges cannot reliably assess.

concepts.name: CI Regression Gate
concepts.explanation: JudgeJudy is deployed as a continuous integration regression gate that blocks AgentX releases at Character.ai if video quality drops below tracked baselines, with automated baseline tracking and regression detection across releases.
concepts.importance: Integrates quality evaluation into the software delivery pipeline, preventing degraded video quality from reaching production users.

concepts.name: Agentic Workflow with Self-Verification
concepts.explanation: The team moved from a rigid sequential pipeline to an agentic workflow where agents validate and self-correct their own outputs before passing video forward in the generation chain.
concepts.importance: Replaces brittle fixed pipelines with adaptive agents that catch and fix their own mistakes, reducing downstream correction costs.

concepts.name: Early Drift Detection (Shift-Left Evaluation)
concepts.explanation: Detecting quality issues at the starting-frame stage or in short six-second clips before they are stitched into long-form video is far cheaper than fixing problems downstream after full generation.
concepts.importance: Front-loads quality checks to minimize wasted compute and manual review, moving evaluation as close to online generation as possible.

concepts.name: Unit Economics of Model Serving
concepts.explanation: Scaling the video quality judge is framed as a unit-economics tradeoff: a small served VLM wins at thousands of evaluations per day, while a slower expert cohort or frontier model may be more accurate but costlier.
concepts.importance: Provides a principled framework for choosing between small/fast and large/accurate models in production based on evaluation volume and cost.

concepts.name: Pluggable Evaluation Harness Architecture
concepts.explanation: JudgeJudy is an open-source harness built in Go that ships as a single binary and can connect arbitrary agents or LLMs as video quality judges with custom rubrics, automated metrics, and human calibration.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates a production-grade, extensible architecture for multimodal evaluation that decouples judge selection from evaluation workflow.

concepts.name: Human Annotation Calibration Pipeline
concepts.explanation: Periodically everyone spends 10–15 minutes annotating videos on random quality axes; this data calibrates AI judges and serves as training data for the next model version, creating an iterative human-in-the-loop improvement cycle.
concepts.importance: Closes the loop between human judgment and automated evaluation, ensuring the judge evolves with changing taste and quality standards.

concepts.name: Telemetry Trace Export
concepts.explanation: The JudgeJudy harness does not yet export all LLM judge traces for integration with external platforms; Bril accepted a feature request to add telemetry trace export capability.
concepts.importance: Highlights the gap between standalone evaluation tools and distributed observability platforms, a known limitation for production traceability.

sections.title: Introduction: the evaluation gap in AI video
sections.summary: Bril introduces the central problem: video generation has become nearly free and visually impressive, but most generated content is still poor—hallucinated limbs, broken physics, hovering. The hard part is not generating video but judging whether it is good enough, and existing tools are borrowed from the text and image eras.

sections.title: Why existing metrics fail for video
sections.summary: CLIP score excels at single-frame evaluation and LPIPS detects inter-frame drift, but neither can judge whether the video tells the intended story, whether physics and pacing make sense, or whether audio is synced to imagery. Video is a storytelling medium and requires evaluation across time.

sections.title: LLM-as-judge and the first benchmark iteration
sections.summary: The team tried LLM-as-judge with foundational models but found them slow, prompt-dependent, and inconsistent. They built a repeatable benchmark combining frame metrics, a consistent LLM judge, and human annotation for calibration, but it was too slow and expensive for near-user generation.

sections.title: Catching drift early is cheaper
sections.summary: Detecting mistakes at the starting-frame stage or in a six-second clip before it is stitched into a long-form video is far cheaper than fixing problems downstream. The goal is to move evals as close to online generation as possible.

sections.title: Distilling experts into a small fast VLM
sections.summary: The committee of expert evaluators was distilled into one small VLM that scores a 15-second video in about 3 seconds and explains why a video is bad. A larger model was more accurate but too slow to justify deployment.

sections.title: Don't score, compare: pairwise preference
sections.summary: Absolute 1–10 scoring produces low inter-rater agreement, but asking which of two videos tells a better story yields high agreement. The team trained on A-vs-B pairs instead of absolute scores.

sections.title: Manufacturing badness and V1's confident failure
sections.summary: Training pairs were created by corrupting good videos and generating random slop. V1 shipped confidently wrong—it scored 9.2 on camera work for a frozen four-second frame and praised physics on hovering ghosts—because it learned to reward gloss and vibe rather than whether the story was actually told.

sections.title: Fixing the dataset: real vs. AI footage pairing
sections.summary: The fix was to pair real footage against AI footage with consistent encoding and identical annotation on both sides, preventing the model from becoming an AI detector. The team also moved from a rigid pipeline to an agentic workflow where agents validate and self-correct their own outputs. Bril's closing advice: go relative, not absolute.

sections.title: Closing advice: score real axes, put eval in the loop
sections.summary: Bril reiterates that comparing video A versus B always gives better results. He urges scoring the real axes you care about—storytelling, pacing, physics—explicitly rather than expecting them to appear. Eval must live inside the generation loop, and ultimately video should be evaluated as a story.

sections.title: Q&A: Evaluating sound and audio-visual sync
sections.summary: Bril uses Atmos for sound quality and intelligibility, and the model learns to identify key frames. When the prompt says 'the door slammed,' the model matches a sound spike at the corresponding timestamp. It does not identify the sound itself but correlates sound spikes with expected key-frame events.

sections.title: Q&A: Lip syncing remains unsolved
sections.summary: Lip syncing is an unsolved problem, especially for animated talking characters whose mouth movement has no real correlation with speech. The team is working on it but has no solution yet.

sections.title: Q&A: Human evaluation and calibration
sections.summary: The Judge Judy harness lets humans annotate any report. Periodically everyone spends 10–15 minutes annotating videos on random axes; this data calibrates AI judges and serves as training data for the next model version. Taste is subjective, so the process evolves over time.

sections.title: Q&A: Why Qwen and scaling economics
sections.summary: Qwen was chosen for strong post-training experience on other use cases; other models were tried but Qwen was good enough. Scaling is a unit-economics tradeoff: the small model can be served as one or many GPU instances, while a slower expert cohort or frontier model like Fable might be better but costlier. For thousands of videos per day the small model wins; for smaller scale, the expert cohort suffices.

sections.title: Q&A: Telemetry and trace export
sections.summary: The Judge Judy repo is a harness that can connect any agents or LLMs. An internal version runs as a service with an agentic harness on top. Bril accepts a feature request to add telemetry trace export for integration with external platforms.

organization.name: Character.ai
organization.summary: Character.ai (Character Technologies Inc., dba Character.ai) is a privately held AI company founded in 2021, registered in Delaware, and headquartered in Menlo Park, CA with offices in Seattle and New York. The company builds consumer AI entertainment products including AI characters, video generation (AvatarFX), Stories, Streams, and an AI Social Feed serving 16M+ monthly active users. CEO Karandeep Anand was appointed in June 2025. The speaker Maor Bril is a Principal Software Engineer at Character.ai, where he builds the agentic platform behind Stories, Streams, and the AI Social Feed, and open-sourced JudgeJudy (a multimodal eval framework gating every AgentX release) and claude-agent-sdk-go. JudgeJudy was open-sourced in March 2026 under the character-ai GitHub organization (MIT license, built in Go).

technologies.label: JudgeJudy Multimodal Evaluation Framework
technologies.summary: JudgeJudy is an open-source multimodal AI evaluation framework built in Go by Character.ai, open-sourced March 2026 under MIT license. It supports AI judges with custom rubrics, automated metrics (BERTScore, CLIP, PESQ), human evaluation with interactive scoring, and a calibration system across text, image, audio, and video modalities. It ships as a single binary, supports 10 providers and 12 metrics, and serves as the CI regression gate for every AgentX release at Character.ai. The harness can connect arbitrary agents or LLMs as video quality judges and supports a pluggable architecture decoupling judge selection from evaluation workflow.
technologies.role: Primary framework and tool demonstrated; the open-source multimodal evaluation harness that gates every AgentX release at Character.ai and connects arbitrary agents or LLMs as video quality judges

technologies.label: Pairwise Preference VLM Judge
technologies.summary: Pairwise preference comparison replaces absolute 1-10 scoring with relative A-vs-B judgments, yielding much higher inter-rater agreement. A small Qwen-family VLM was distilled from a committee of expert evaluators and trained with Bradley-Terry loss on pairs of real and deliberately corrupted footage, scoring 15-second videos in approximately 3 seconds while explaining why a video is bad rather than returning only a binary verdict. V1 was confidently wrong: it scored 9.2 on camera work for a four-second frozen frame and praised physics on hovering ghosts, because it learned to reward gloss and vibe rather than substance. The fix paired real footage against AI footage with consistent encoding and identical annotation to prevent the model from becoming an AI detector.
technologies.role: Central technique demonstrated; the distilled VLM judge trained on pairwise preferences with Bradley-Terry loss is the main engineering contribution described in the talk

technologies.label: Frame-Level Video Metrics
technologies.summary: CLIP score and LPIPS are existing image-era metrics borrowed for video evaluation but found fundamentally insufficient. CLIP score excels at evaluating individual frames by measuring visual-text embedding alignment but misses temporal incoherence. LPIPS detects inter-frame drift by measuring perceptual distance between consecutive frames but cannot assess whether a video tells a coherent story, whether physics and pacing make sense, or whether audio is synced to imagery. The talk argues that video is fundamentally a storytelling medium requiring evaluation across story fidelity, physics, pacing, character consistency, and audio-visual synchronization, none of which these frame-level metrics can capture.
technologies.role: Contrastive baseline metrics discussed as insufficient; they motivate the need for the pairwise preference VLM judge and the JudgeJudy evaluation framework

technologies.label: Audio-Visual Synchronization Evaluation
technologies.summary: Audio-visual synchronization evaluation combines Atmos for sound quality assessment with key-frame timestamp spike matching for synchronization. When the prompt says 'the door slammed,' the model looks for a sound spike at the corresponding key-frame timestamp rather than identifying the sound itself. This approach correlates sound spikes with expected key-frame events to detect desynchronization. Lip syncing remains an unsolved problem, especially for animated talking characters whose mouth movement has no real correlation with speech audio.
technologies.role: Secondary evaluation capability discussed in Q&A; extends the evaluation methodology to the audio dimension and identifies lip syncing as an unsolved frontier problem
